title: Exposure to health misinformation about COVID-19 and increased tobacco and alcohol use: a population-based survey in Hong Kong
screen_reason: Population-based random-sample telephone/web survey of 1,501 Hong Kong adults (April 2020) that asked whether respondents had ever seen the claim that smoking/alcohol drinking protects against COVID-19 on named social networking platforms. 19.0% (282/1,501, 95% CI 16.8-21.4) reported such exposure, and a second false claim used as a negative control ('drinking tea can protect against COVID-19') gave 17.0% (242/1,501). Both are self-reported shares of respondents who encountered a specific false health claim, with stated denominators -> RECALL (exposure). The paper's aim (behavioural consequences) is not the eligibility test; the descriptive share is reported.

estimates.platform: Social networking sites named in the item: WhatsApp/WeChat, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and online forums (including Telegram)
estimates.measure_type: % of adults who report ever having seen claims that 'smoking/alcohol drinking can protect against COVID-19' on social networking sites
estimates.denominator: 1,501 randomly sampled Chinese-speaking Hong Kong residents aged 18+ (500 by landline random-digit dialling with next-birthday household selection, 1,001 from a population-representative mobile panel of over 100,000 users); prevalence weighted by sex, age and education to the Hong Kong general adult population
estimates.definition: Answered yes to having ever seen claims that 'smoking/alcohol drinking can protect against COVID-19' from WhatsApp/WeChat, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter or online forums (including Telegram)
estimates.misinfo_def: "unproven claims that smoking and alcohol drinking could protect against COVID-19"; "Inaccurate or unproven claims that smoking and alcohol drinking could protect against COVID-19 has been circulating online, despite the WHO's warnings about the lack of evidence."
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 2; also Abstract (Results) and 'What this paper adds'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is self-reported: respondents were asked whether they had ever seen the claim on WhatsApp/WeChat, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter or online forums (including Telegram). The claim itself was designated health misinformation by the authors on the basis of WHO statements on tobacco use and on alcohol in relation to COVID-19; no coder reliability applies (single self-report item).

estimates.notes: SINGLE-CLAIM measure, not a general misinformation-exposure measure: 19.0% is exposure to one specific (double-barrelled) claim on one set of platforms, so it is a floor for COVID-19 misinformation exposure in this population, not an estimate of it. The item is compound ('smoking/alcohol drinking'), so a respondent exposed to only one half is counted the same as one exposed to both. Exposure through traditional media was not asked, which the authors note would misclassify some exposed respondents as unexposed. platform_norm coded multi_platform because the item explicitly enumerates five social platforms; a coder treating the instrument rather than the exposure locus as the platform would code 'survey'. breadth coded 'false' - the claim is contradicted by WHO evidence statements - though the paper's own hedge is 'unproven'. Value is the weighted estimate; the unweighted share is 282/1501 = 18.8%. | QUOTE NOTE: the text file is a de-columnised two-column PDF, so the sentence is split across text lines; source_quote is the longest contiguous verbatim span carrying the value. In full: 'Of the 1501 respondents, 282 (19.0%; 95% CI 16.8% to 21.4%) reported having seen claims that ‘smoking/alcohol drinking can protect against COVID-19’ from social networking sites.' moderator_quote in full: 'Respondents were asked if they had ever seen claims that ‘smoking/alcohol drinking can protect against COVID-19’ from WhatsApp/WeChat, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and online forums (including Telegram).' | ground_truth coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL (the numerator is what respondents say they saw); the stimulus claim was pre-designated false by the authors against WHO guidance, which an adjudicator may want to note.

estimates.notes: FLAGGED FOR ADJUDICATION. This is a second false COVID-19 protection claim, measured on the same respondents with the same instrument, so it is a legitimate exposure prevalence in its own right - but the authors introduce it as a methodological control, not as a misinformation-exposure finding, and it must NEVER be pooled with the 19.0% row: the two rows share the same 1,501 respondents and overlap by an unreported amount. definition_variant flagged true for that reason. An adjudicator who wants one estimate per paper should keep the 19.0% row and drop this one. Unweighted share is 242/1501 = 16.1% against a reported (presumably weighted) 17.0%. | QUOTE NOTE: two-column PDF, sentence split across text lines. In full: 'In the sensitivity analysis, exposure to claims that ‘drinking tea can protect against COVID-19’ (17.0%; 242 of 1501) showed no significant association with self-reported change in tobacco and alcohol consumption (all p>0.11).' moderator_quote in full: 'We repeated the regressions by modelling ‘drinking tea can protect against COVID-19’ as the exposure variable, which should show no association with the outcomes (negative exposure control).' | ground_truth coded self_report per the RECALL rule.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Platform-level exposure counts are given without denominators or percentages: 'Leading sources of exposure were WhatsApp/WeChat (n=149) and Facebook (n=138), followed by online forums (n=64), Instagram (n=37) and Twitter (n=6)'. These are multiple-response counts among the 282 exposed respondents; converting them to shares of 1,501 or of 282 would be my own arithmetic on a multiple-response item and is not defensible, so no platform-split rows. (2) Behaviour-change shares are outcomes, not misinformation prevalence: '15.6% (48 of 280) of current tobacco users and 5.5% (42 of 722) of alcohol users reported having increased their consumption', with reductions of 19.1% (49/280) and 36.8% (244/722). (3) Table 1's weighted percentages (e.g. 33.3% of tobacco users who increased consumption were exposed) are exposure shares WITHIN behaviour-change strata, i.e. the reverse conditional, and the paper explicitly notes the sample was too small for subgroup analysis; not extracted. (4) Odds ratios (2.37 for tobacco, 4.16 for alcohol) are association measures, not shares. (5) Bivariate correlates of exposure (male sex, younger age, higher education, all p<0.001) are reported only in an online supplementary table not present in this text.

rob.design: Population-based cross-sectional survey (Hong Kong COVID-19 Health Information Survey, CoVHInS), fielded 9-23 April 2020, design adapted from the authors' Family and Health Information Trend Survey. Sampling frame: Chinese-speaking Hong Kong residents aged 18+, sampled by two probability routes - landline random-digit dialling from the Government numbering plan with second-stage next-birthday selection within the household (n=500), and a random draw from a research agency's population-representative panel of over 100,000 mobile phone users with no second-stage selection (n=1,001), total N=1,501, 47.5% male. Response rates: 61.3% (500 of 816) landline, 61.7% (1,001 of 1,623) mobile. Target of 1,500 set to give a margin of error of +/-2.5% for a 50% prevalence at 95% confidence. Data collection: computer-assisted telephone interviewing by trained interviewers (landline) or self-administered web questionnaire reached by SMS/email link (mobile); questionnaire refined by cognitive interviewing with 10 persons; a random one-fifth of landline interview records audited. Weighting: prevalences weighted by sex, age and education to the Hong Kong general adult population. No missing data; complete-case analysis. Analysis: multinomial logistic regression (no change as base outcome) adjusted for survey method, sex, age, education, mutual tobacco/alcohol use status, home isolation days and PHQ-4 distress, with a pre-specified negative exposure control that behaved as expected (all p>0.11). Stata/MP 15.1; two-sided alpha 0.05. Ethics: University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority HK West Cluster IRB UW 20-238; informed consent from all respondents. No content coding, so no inter-rater reliability applies. Authors' limitations: cross-sectional design, self-reported exposure and outcomes, small subsamples precluding demographic subgroup analysis, and exposure via non-social-media outlets not measured (biasing associations towards the null). Additional note: the exposure item is double-barrelled ('smoking/alcohol drinking'), which the paper does not discuss.
